comparator.name: Dutch Languages and Cultures — Dutch Language and Culture
comparator.sourceNotes: The programme-specific 2026–27 Teaching and Examination Regulations define two formal tracks. The registry target expressly names the Dutch Language and Culture route, so that route is selected independently of UCR fit. For students beginning in September 2026, the regulation gives a coherent 60+60+60=180 EC curriculum: 60 EC of named first-year components, 60 EC of named second-year components, and a third year comprising a genuine 30-EC minor, a 10-EC faculty-wide module, a 10-EC thesis, and two named 5-EC components. The regulation states that the second- and third-year parts of this new curriculum take effect in 2027–28 and 2028–29 respectively; they are the prescribed continuation of the 2026 entry cohort rather than a mixture of concurrent-cohort tables. The minor is retained as open curricular space and no optional minor subject is presented as compulsory. CP198 is the retained active owner of the named Dutch track. CP199 is a permanently retained alias for the same track; its source row 212, variant offering and historical interest evidence now map to CP198 alongside source row 211 and the predecessor offering. Raw names, codes and interest texts are preserved; old 56804 remains provenance rather than a current additional degree. The generic CP200 umbrella remains a separate broader normalized target. The adopted OER and current degree identity were rechecked on 2026-10-08; the original UCR assessment date and evidence remain. The live programme page and the 2026–2027 regulations were rechecked on 2026-10-14; the settled target-specific route and 180-EC reconstruction remain unchanged. routeSelection.basis: The University of Groningen regulation distinguishes Dutch Language and Culture and Frisian Language and Culture. The normalized registry target itself names Dutch Language and Culture, so this formal route is selected before and independently of evaluating any UCR course fit. The route's genuine 30-EC minor remains open rather than being populated with an invented specialization.

core: Dutch-language literature from the Middle Ages to the present, literary interpretation, creative writing and the relationship between literature and society
Dutch language structure, change, meaning, variation, rhetoric, writing and public communication
Language acquisition, cognition and critical analysis of digital communication
Dutch culture, social identity, mediated narratives and contemporary social questions
Qualitative, literary, linguistic and statistical methods culminating in a Dutch Studies thesis
adjacent: Language, cognition and public communication: acquisition, variation, persuasion, debate and digital discourse
Literature, writing and culture: historical texts, creative practice, performance, society and mediated identity
Digital and empirical methods for studying language, texts and communication
questions: How do language, rhetoric and media shape identity, politics and public debate?
How do literary texts and stories interpret society across historical periods and media?
How do narratives and mediated identities connect literature, cultural memory and contemporary society?

alternatives.label: Literature, language & public communication
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum balances literature, communication, language processing, media and research. The label does not claim a full Dutch Studies or advanced Dutch-language curriculum.
alternatives.concept: A related-fields response combining literary interpretation, rhetoric, stylistics, public communication, media, psycholinguistics, one introductory Dutch-language course, digital methods and independent humanities research. It does not reproduce Groningen’s advanced Dutch linguistics, proficiency or period-specific Dutch literature sequence.
progression: Introductory literature, rhetoric, Dutch communication, brain and behaviour, history, sociology, media, programming and research methods precede advanced literary, cultural, communication, data and psycholinguistic work. All prerequisites and planned-semester constraints are satisfied; seven courses are level 3.

alternatives.label: Language, cognition & digital society
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum concentrates on language acquisition and use, rhetoric, media, social identity, AI ethics, data analysis and language technologies without presenting these as Dutch linguistics.
alternatives.concept: A language-use pathway centred on acquisition and psycholinguistics, rhetoric and persuasion, public and digital communication, social variation and identity, AI ethics, data analysis and language technologies, with one introductory Dutch-language course.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the integrated closest response, four courses (30 EC) replace literary and historical study with AI ethics, advanced social theory, identity-focused psychology and neural networks. The change follows the explicit language-use, social-identity and digital-communication evidence.
progression: Dutch communication, rhetoric, literature, brain and behaviour, sociology, history, media, programming, data science and Mathematical Methods precede advanced social theory, persuasive communication, psycholinguistics and neural-network study. Mathematical Methods is completed before its dependent Neural Networks course; all formal prerequisites and planned-semester constraints are satisfied, with eight level-3 courses.

alternatives.label: Literature, culture & social questions
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by literary interpretation, media, historical context, cultural identity, adaptation, material circulation and socially engaged cultural analysis.
alternatives.concept: A literature-and-culture pathway centred on close reading, historical texts and identities, literary circulation across media, adaptation, environmental and social questions, cultural institutions and creative communication, with one introductory Dutch-language course.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest response, six courses (45 EC) replace psycholinguistics, statistics, programming, data science and advanced historical research with media archaeology, environmental media, documentary and denser art-historical study. It differs by ten courses (75 EC) from the language-and-digital-society route.
progression: Introductory literature, film/media, rhetoric, Dutch communication, history, art history, sociology and qualitative methods precede advanced literary meaning, adaptation, documentary, media and race, creative communication and art-historical research. All formal prerequisites and planned-semester constraints are satisfied; eight courses are level 3.

selection.assessment: The closest related-fields response integrates literature, rhetoric, language processing, public communication, media and research. Two additional generator-backed directions are coherent and feasible: language, cognition and digital society, and literature, culture and social questions. The closest and language routes differ by four courses (30 EC), the closest and literature routes by six (45 EC), and the two focused routes by ten (75 EC). All three preserve the absence of a full Dutch linguistics, proficiency and period-specific Dutch literature sequence.

blocks: Introduction to Literary Studies directly develops close reading and interpretation across literary genres, but not specifically in Dutch.
Great Literary Works gives chronological literary interpretation that includes medieval texts; it does not reproduce medieval Dutch literature.
Life & Travel Writing develops historical and cultural literary analysis, but not a dedicated early-modern Dutch sequence.
Film & Text provides advanced narrative, adaptation and textual analysis related to modern literary study, without Dutch-period specialization.
Perspectives on Literary Meaning combines theoretical approaches with a research project and is the strongest scheduled counterpart to literary research approaches.
Introduction to Brain & Behavior supplies cognitive foundations for text and language processing.
The Art of Rhetorical Communication directly studies rhetoric, argument and audience, without the comparator’s Dutch-language stylistics depth.
Style & Meaning analyses linguistic choices and meaning in texts; it is general stylistics rather than Dutch semantics.
Dutch develops introductory oral and written Dutch communication; it does not equal advanced academic language-proficiency development.
Persuasive Communication directly studies persuasion, framing and argumentation.
Creative Communication Laboratory studies and practises creative meaning-making through language and media, while not being Dutch creative-writing training.
Psycholinguistics directly studies language acquisition, processing and experimental methods, but not Dutch-specific acquisition.
Methods, thesis, specialist gaps & open minor
Research Methods & Statistics supplies research design and quantitative foundations related to the programme’s research workshops.

notes.text: Groningen provides a Dutch-language disciplinary sequence in Dutch phonology, syntax, semantics, language change and proficiency, Dutch literature across historical periods, research workshops and a Dutch Studies thesis. UCR can build coherent related programmes through literature, rhetoric, communication, media, psycholinguistics, history and digital methods, including one introductory Dutch-language course, but these do not reproduce a full Neerlandistiek curriculum.

UCR lacks the comparator’s cumulative Dutch phonology and syntax, historical Dutch, advanced Dutch-language proficiency, period-specific Dutch literature sequence and compulsory Dutch Studies thesis. Its adjacent analytical and research strengths must be read with those specialist gaps visible.
